Meanwhile, every application eventually discovers that its database cannot answer the same question thousands of times per second without strain. A cache sits between the code and the storage layer, holding recent results in memory so repeated reads return quickly.

However, caching introduces a hard problem: stale data. When a row changes, any cached copy becomes wrong until it expires or is invalidated; choosing between short time-to-live values and explicit invalidation is a real engineering tradeoff. Teams often start with simple expiry, then add targeted eviction once they understand which queries matter most for correctness.

Along with that, a lookup tool must stay small and fast; storing too much in RAM can hurt, so most shops cap growth and drop old rows first. Monitoring hit ratios daily shows if this plan is working or falling short.

Finally, a well-tuned cache pays for itself many times over; measure carefully, invalidate deliberately, and the caching work is done.
